verses.zh: 这事以后，有人告诉约瑟说：「你的父亲病了。」他就带着两个儿子玛拿西和以法莲同去。
verses.en: After these things Joseph was told,[NOTE:1] “Your father is weakening.” So he took his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim with him.
notes: Heb “and one said.” With no expressed subject in the Hebrew text, the verb can be translated with the passive voice.
verses.commentary:
48:1 "Joseph was told" The Rabbinical Midrash says that Ephraim studied regularly with his grandfather
Jacob and he is the one who told Joseph, but this is typical of rabbinical comments that are based on a
supposition, not contextual or textual information. It is always fair to ask those who claim to speak for
God, "Show me where you got this from Scripture."

▣ "So he took his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim with him" These boys were half-Egyptian, but
apparently this is setting the stage for the patriarchal blessing (i.e., adoption) which would include
them as full heirs (i.e., Gen. 48:8-22).

verses.zh: 有人告诉雅各说：「请看，你儿子约瑟到你这里来了。」以色列就勉强在床上坐起来。
verses.en: When Jacob was told,[NOTE:1] “Your son Joseph has just[NOTE:2] come to you,” Israel regained strength and sat up on his bed.
notes: Heb “and one told and said.” The verbs have no expressed subject and can be translated with the passive voice.
Heb “Look, your son Joseph.”

verses.zh: 雅各对约瑟说：「全能的　神曾在迦南地的路斯向我显现，赐福与我，
verses.en: Jacob said to Joseph, “The Sovereign God[NOTE:1] appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me.
notes: Heb “El Shaddai.” See the extended note on the phrase “Sovereign God” in Gen 17:1.
verses.commentary:
48:3 "Jacob said to Joseph, 'God Almighty'" This is the traditional patriarchal name for God
(cf. Exod. 6:3). It is El Shaddai; El from the general name for God from the root "to be
strong" and Shaddai, which seems to mean "the all-sufficient One." See full note at Gen. 12:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI

▣ "appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me" Luz is the Canaanite name for
Bethel (cf. Gen. 28:17, 19; 35:9-15). Apparently, as YHWH had blessed Jacob, Jacob was now going to bless
Joseph's sons. It is interesting to note that, as godly a man as Joseph was, YHWH never appeared to him as
He did to the Patriarchs (see note at Gen. 46:2), which shows that even this literary unit concerning Joseph
is really in the larger section on the life of Jacob.

verses.zh: 对我说：『我必使你生养众多，成为多民，又要把这地赐给你的后裔，永远为业。』
verses.en: He said to me, ‘I am going to make you fruitful[NOTE:1] and will multiply you.[NOTE:2] I will make you into a group of nations, and I will give this land to your descendants[NOTE:3] as an everlasting possession.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Look, I am making you fruitful.” The participle following הִנֵּה (hinneh) has the nuance of a certain and often imminent future.
The perfect verbal form with vav consecutive carries on the certain future idea.
The Hebrew text adds “after you,” which has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

The Hebrew word אֲחֻזָּה (ʾakhuzzah), translated “possession,” describes a permanent holding in the land. It is the noun form of the same verb (אָחַז, ʾakhaz) that was used for the land given to them in Goshen (Gen 47:27).
verses.commentary:
48:4 "I will make you fruitful and numerous" There are three specific blessings here which are related
to the Abrahamic blessing of Genesis:

- I will make you fruitful and numerous

- I will make you a company of peoples

- I will give the land to your descendants

It is interesting that Jacob leaves out the clause from Gen. 35:11 (line 5), "and kings shall
come forth from you," because apparently that aspect was for Judah (cf. Gen. 49:10). Prosperity and abundance
would characterize the family, but kings would come from Judah (i.e., Messiah, Isa. 9:6-7; Micah 5:2).

48:4

NASB, NRSV
"company of peoples"

NKJV
"multitude of people"

TEV
"many nations"

NJB
"an assembly of peoples"

REB
"a host of nations"

JPSOA
"a company of peoples"

LXX
"gathering of nations"

Peshitta
"a multitude of peoples"

This refers to YHWH's promises of many descendants in Gen. 28:3; 35:11. This large
multitude is ofter referred to by "dust," "stars," and "sand." See full note at Gen. 15:5.

▣ "for an everlasting possession" This is the Hebrew term 'olam. It must be interpreted
in light of the context. When one remembers the exilic period it is obvious that this term does not mean
to perpetuity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('OLAM)

verses.zh: 我未到埃及见你之先，你在埃及地所生的以法莲和玛拿西这两个儿子是我的，正如流便和西缅是我的一样。
verses.en: “Now, as for your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, they will be mine.[NOTE:1] Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine just as Reuben and Simeon are.
notes: They will be mine. Jacob is here adopting his two grandsons Manasseh and Ephraim as his sons, and so they will have equal share with the other brothers. They will be in the place of Joseph and Levi (who will become a priestly tribe) in the settlement of the land. See I. Mendelsohn, “A Ugaritic Parallel to the Adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh,” IEJ (1959): 180-83.
verses.commentary:
48:5 "are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are" It is interesting that
in Gen. 48:1 Manasseh is mentioned before Ephraim, but from Gen. 48:5 and Gen. 48:14 Ephraim will appear
before Manasseh. This seems to be planned by Jacob (cf. Gen. 48:13-14). Ephraim and Manasseh are going to
replace Simeon and Reuben as the firstborn, pre-imminent heirs of Jacob (cf. 1 Chr. 5:1). The younger Ephraim
will be the stronger of the two. This does not affect Judah's leadership of the family (cf. 1 Chr. 5:2)! This
is as much a discipline of Reuben (cf. Gen. 35:22; 49:4; 1 Chr. 5:1) and Simeon (cf. Gen. 34:25; 49:5-7) as
it was an inclusion for Joseph's sons. Not only is there reversal in expectation between Manasseh and Ephraim
(as there was with Esau and Jacob), but this same reversal of expectation will occur between Joseph and Judah
(cf. Gen. 49:8-12). Joseph was the obvious choice for family leadership, but the choice was YHWH's, not the
culture (i.e., remember David and his brothers).

verses.zh: 你在他们以后所生的就是你的，他们可以归于他们弟兄的名下得产业。
verses.en: Any children that you father[NOTE:1] after them will be yours; they will be listed[NOTE:2] under the names of their brothers in their inheritance.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “you fathered.”
Heb “called” or “named.”
Listed under the names of their brothers in their inheritance. This means that any subsequent children of Joseph will be incorporated into the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.
verses.commentary:
48:6 "But your offspring that have been born after them" This implies that Joseph may have more
children, but if he did we have no record of them in the Bible.

verses.zh: 至于我，我从巴旦来的时候，拉结死在我眼前，在迦南地的路上，离以法他还有一段路程，我就把她葬在以法他的路上〈以法他就是伯利恒〉。」
verses.en: But as for me, when I was returning from Paddan, Rachel died—to my sorrow[NOTE:1]—in the land of Canaan. It happened along the way, some distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there on the way to Ephrath” (that is, Bethlehem).[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “upon me, against me,” which might mean something like “to my sorrow.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map7-E2; Map8-E2; Map10-B4.
verses.commentary:
48:7 This is a historical summary about Joseph's mother. Rachel's death was painful and shocking to
Jacob. He saw these two grandsons of Rachel's first son, Joseph, as somehow coming from Rachel herself. They
would be considered full "sons" (in an inheritance sense) of Rachel. She would be happy for this even in the
afterlife!

48:7

NASB, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA
"Paddan"

NKJV
"Padan"

REB, Peshitta
"Paddan-aram"

LXX
"Mesopotamia of Syria"

The UBS Text Project, p. 75, gives the MT option (NASB) an "A" rating. However, there is
some doubt about the meaning of the word (BDB 804). Many assert it is a general name for

- the area around Haran, but this depends on an Arabic root and an assumed Aramaic root. The root
normally denotes "a yoke," and not "a field" or "plain."

- a "road" or "highway" from an Akkadian root which closely resembles "Haran"

Both options point toward a northern Mesopotamian locale (cf. Gen. 25:20; 28:2; 23:18).

verses.zh: 以色列看见约瑟的两个儿子，就说：「这是谁？」
verses.en: When Israel saw Joseph’s sons, he asked, “Who are these?”
verses.commentary:
48:8 "When Israel saw Joseph's sons" We learn from Gen. 48:10 that his eyesight was very bad, but
not completely gone. Jacob (remembering his trickery of his father) wants to be sure who he is blessing!

verses.zh: 约瑟对他父亲说：「这是　神在这里赐给我的儿子。」以色列说：「请你领他们到我跟前，我要给他们祝福。」
verses.en: Joseph said to his father, “They are the[NOTE:1] sons God has given me in this place.” His father[NOTE:2] said, “Bring them to me so I may bless them.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “my.”
Heb “and he”; the referent (Joseph’s father) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The cohortative with prefixed vav (ו) indicates purpose after the imperative.
verses.commentary:
48:9 "Joseph said to his father, 'They are my sons, whom God has given me here'" The rabbis say that
Joseph had to show his marriage license to Jacob to convince his father that his wife had become a convert.
However, to me it seems that this verse is emphasizing the fact that in all areas, Joseph saw the hand of
God in his life.

▣ "Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them" The two VERBS are

- bring/take, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

- bless, BDB 138, KB 159, Piel IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE
sense

The term "bless" has a fuller and more theological sense here. It involves the metaphorical
adoption of these two grandsons into full inheritance rights as Jacob's own sons. There are now thirteen
tribes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLESSING (OT)

verses.zh: 以色列年纪老迈，眼睛昏花，不能看见。约瑟领他们到他跟前，他就和他们亲嘴，抱着他们。
verses.en: Now Israel’s eyes were failing[NOTE:1] because of his age; he was not able to see well. So Joseph[NOTE:2] brought his sons[NOTE:3] near to him, and his father[NOTE:4] kissed them and embraced them.
notes: Heb “heavy.”sn The disjunctive clause provides supplemental information that is important to the story. The weakness of Israel’s sight is one of several connections between this chapter and Gen 27. Here there are two sons, and it appears that the younger is being blessed over the older by a blind old man. While it was by Jacob’s deception in chap. 27, here it is with Jacob’s full knowledge.
Heb “he”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “them”; the referent (Joseph’s sons) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and he”; the referent (Joseph’s father) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
48:10 "he kissed them and embraced them" This was a special bonding as well as a legal (cf. Gen. 48:12)
experience.

verses.zh: 以色列对约瑟说：「我想不到得见你的面，不料，　神又使我得见你的儿子。」
verses.en: Israel said to Joseph, “I never expected[NOTE:1] to see you[NOTE:2] again, but now God has allowed me to see your children[NOTE:3] too.”
notes: On the meaning of the Hebrew verb פָּלַל (palal) here, see E. A. Speiser, “The Stem pll in Hebrew,” JBL 82 (1963): 301-6. Speiser argues that this verb means “to estimate” as in Exod 21:22.
Heb “your face.”
Heb “offspring.”

verses.zh: 约瑟把两个儿子从以色列两膝中领出来，自己就脸伏于地下拜。
verses.en: So Joseph moved them from Israel’s knees[NOTE:1] and bowed down with his face to the ground.
notes: Heb “and Joseph brought them out from with his knees.” The two boys had probably been standing by Israel’s knees when being adopted and blessed. The referent of the pronoun “his” (Israel) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
48:12

NASB, NRSV
"took them from his knees"

NKJV
"brought them from beside his knees"

TEV, REB
"took them from Jacob's lap"

LXX
"brought them out from between his knees"

Peshitta
"removed them from before his knees"

JPSOA
"them removed them from his knees"

This was an adoption rite, which is alluded to in Gen. 48:5. Passing the children under
the loins seems to have been the manner for this ancient adoption process (i.e., as women gave birth through
their knees, Gen. 30:3; Job 3:17, JB footnote, p. 73). See IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 76,
for examples from the Code of Hammurabi and Ugaritic literature.

verses.zh: 随后，约瑟又拉着他们两个，以法莲在他的右手里，对着以色列的左手，玛拿西在他的左手里，对着以色列的右手，领他们到以色列的跟前。
verses.en: Joseph positioned them;[NOTE:1] he put Ephraim on his right hand across from Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh on his left hand across from Israel’s right hand. Then Joseph brought them closer to his father.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and Joseph took the two of them.”
Heb “and he brought near to him.” The referents of the pronouns “he” and “him” (Joseph and his father respectively) have been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 以色列伸出右手来，按在以法莲的头上〈以法莲乃是次子〉，又剪搭过左手来，按在玛拿西的头上〈玛拿西原是长子〉。
verses.en: Israel stretched out his right hand and placed it on Ephraim’s head, although he was the younger.[NOTE:1] Crossing his hands, he put his left hand on Manasseh’s head, for Manasseh was the firstborn.
notes: The disjunctive clause is circumstantial-concessive here.
verses.commentary:
48:14 "But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim" This is the aspect
of crossing his hands so that his right hand-the hand of pre-imminence-would bless the younger son who would
have the pre-imminence over his brother (as Jacob and Esau). The reversal of the culturally expected option
(cf. Gen. 48:18) shows God's control and sovereignty (cf. Gen. 48:19). This is the first biblical account of
blessing in association with the laying on of hands. From this point forward it will become a regular
practice.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAYING ON OF
HANDS IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRSTBORN

verses.zh: 他就给约瑟祝福说：「愿我祖亚伯拉罕和我父以撒所事奉的　神，就是一生牧养我直到今日的　神，
verses.en: Then he blessed Joseph and said, “May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked—the God who has been my shepherd[NOTE:1] all my life long to this day,
notes: Heb “shepherded me.” The verb has been translated as an English noun for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
48:15-16 Verses 15-16 are a supplement to the family blessing recorded in Genesis 49. In Jacob's
final blessing to the whole family he does not mention Joseph's two sons by name (cf. Gen. 49:22-26). This
blessing is in poetic form (as is Gen. 48:20). Notice the threefold designation of God. God is seen as

- the patriarchal God

- the Shepherd

- the Angel

It is obvious that the angel of Gen. 48:16 must be the Angel of the Lord who is a physical
manifestation (cf. Gen. 16:7-13; 18:2,16,17-21,22-23; 22:11-15; 31:11,13; 48:15-16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD

48:15 "He blessed Joseph" Obviously these two boys (Gen. 48:16) were receiving the patriarchal blessing
of Joseph (Gen. 48:15). From Genesis 49 it seems that Joseph was receiving the double inheritance rights
(cf. Gen. 49:22-26) of the firstborn, while Judah was to receive the Messianic line (cf. Gen. 49:8-12).

▣ "walked" This VERB (BDB 229, KB 246, Hithpael PERFECT) is
often a metaphor for lifestyle faith (cf. Gen. 5:22,24; 6:9; 24:40; Eph. 4:1,17; 5:2,15). God demands it
(cf. Gen. 17:1). God wants a people who reflect His character to a lost and needy world (i.e., the nations).
The Patriarchs, with all their imperfections, lived before YHWH in an obedient, repentant, faithful way!

To put it another way, eternal life has observable characteristics. We are saved, not just
to be with God when we die, but to be with God now! The goal of biblical faith is Christlikeness now
(i.e., Rom. 8:28-29; Eph. 1:4; 2:10; 4:13)! The Bible's covenants have requirements.

- faith (initial and daily)

- repentance (initial and daily)

- obedience (lifestyle)

- perseverance through life

These are summarized in Deut. 8:6; 19:9; 26:17; 28:9; 30:16!

verses.zh: 救赎我脱离一切患难的那使者，赐福与这两个童子。愿他们归在我的名下和我祖亚伯拉罕、我父以撒的名下。又愿他们在世界中生养众多。」
verses.en: the angel[NOTE:1] who has protected me[NOTE:2] from all harm—bless these boys.May my name be named in them,[NOTE:3] and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac.May they grow into a multitude on the earth.”
notes: Smr reads “king” here, but the traditional reading (“angel”) may be maintained. Jacob closely associates God with an angelic protective presence. This does not mean that Jacob viewed his God as a mere angel, but it does suggest that he was aware of an angelic presence sent by God to protect him. Here he so closely associates the two that they become virtually indistinguishable. In this culture messengers typically carried the authority of the one who sent them and could even be addressed as such. Perhaps Jacob thought that the divine blessing would be mediated through this angelic messenger.

The verb גָּאַל (gaʾal) has the basic idea of “protect” as a near relative might do. It is used for buying someone out of bondage, marrying a deceased brother’s widow, paying off debts, avenging the family, and the like. The meanings of “deliver, protect, avenge” are most fitting when God is the subject (see A. R. Johnson, “The Primary Meaning of גאל,” Congress Volume: Copenhagen, 1953 [VTSup], 67-77).
Or “be recalled through them.”
verses.commentary:
48:16 "who has redeemed me from all evil" This is the term Go'el (BDB 145 I, KB 169, Qal
PARTICIPLE, cf. Exod. 6:6; 15:13), which is used for the kinsmen redeemer (Ruth 4:6) or blood
avenger (cf. Deut. 19:6; Jos. 20:3). It refers to that near kin who avenged or bought one back either from
slavery, financial ruin, or as a prisoner of war. This term also occurs in Ruth 4:6; Num. 5:8; 1 Kgs. 16:11;
Job 19:25.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RANSOM/REDEEM

▣ "And may my name live on in them" This may refer to the ancient view that a man lived on in
his children (i.e., 2 Sam. 18:18; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 677), or more likely, that the covenant faith of Jacob
(cf. Gen. 48:16, line 3) would be passed on to these two boys.

The last three verbs of Gen. 48:16 are IMPERFECTS used in a
JUSSIVE sense (i.e., "let. . .")

- bless, BDB 138, KB 159, Piel IMPERFECT

- be called, BDB 894, KB 1128, Niphal IMPERFECT

- grow, BDB 185, KB 213, Qal IMPERFECT

verses.zh: 约瑟见他父亲把右手按在以法莲的头上，就不喜悦，便提起他父亲的手，要从以法莲头上挪到玛拿西的头上。
verses.en: When Joseph saw that his father placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, it displeased him.[NOTE:1] So he took his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.
notes: Heb “it was bad in his eyes.”
verses.commentary:
48:17 "it displeased him" This VERB in the Qal stem (BDB 949, KB 1269, Qal
IMPERFECT with waw) is a strong VERB denoting Joseph's feeling about
this reversal. The VERB can describe

- distress, Gen. 21:11,12

- displeasure, Num. 11:10; Jos. 24:15; 1 Sam. 8:6; 18:8; 2 Sam. 11:25; Neh. 2:10

- grief, Deut. 15:10; 1 Sam. 1:8; Neh. 2:3

- hostility, Deut. 15:9; 28:54,56

- evil, Gen. 38:10; 2 Sam. 11:27

- went ill with, Ps. 106:32; 2 Sam. 20:6

Obviously #2 fits this context best, but it is a strong word. Joseph's feelings about what
Jacob did were not a minor issue! He interrupted the blessing in an attempt to move Jacob's hand. Even
Joseph did not always know the Lord's will. Jacob, not Joseph, is the Patriarch of the covenant family.

verses.zh: 约瑟对他父亲说：「我父，不是这样。这本是长子，求你把右手按在他的头上。」
verses.en: Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father, for this is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”

verses.zh: 他父亲不从，说：「我知道，我儿，我知道。他也必成为一族，也必昌大。只是他的兄弟将来比他还大；他兄弟的后裔要成为多族。」
verses.en: But his father refused and said, “I know, my son, I know. He too will become a nation and he too will become great. In spite of this, his younger brother will be even greater and his descendants will become a multitude[NOTE:1] of nations.”
notes: Heb “fullness.”
verses.commentary:
48:19 The VERB "I know" (BDB 393, KB 390, two Qal PERFECTS) is
repeated twice for emphasis. Jacob knew what he was doing (apparently by divine leadership). The reversal
of expectations would continue.

verses.zh: 当日就给他们祝福说：「以色列人要指着你们祝福说：『愿　神使你如以法莲、玛拿西一样。』」于是立以法莲在玛拿西以上。
verses.en: So he blessed them that day, saying, “By you[NOTE:1] will Israel bless,[NOTE:2] saying,‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’”Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.[NOTE:3]
notes: The pronoun is singular in the Hebrew text, apparently elevating Ephraim as the more prominent of the two. Note, however, that both are named in the blessing formula that follows.
Or “pronounce a blessing.”

On the elevation of Ephraim over Manasseh see E. C. Kingsbury, “He Set Ephraim Before Manasseh,” HUCA 38 (1967): 129-36; H. Mowvley, “The Concept and Content of ‘Blessing’ in the Old Testament,” BT 16 (1965): 74-80; and I. Mendelsohn, “On the Preferential Status of the Eldest Son,” BASOR 156 (1959): 38-40.
verses.commentary:
48:20 "Israel" The "he" of line 1 refers to Jacob/Israel (i.e., SINGULAR, but Israel
in the second line could refer to the nation (a collective, cf. TEV).

▣ "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh" This is going to be a blessing proverb which
was used by the people of God.

verses.zh: 以色列又对约瑟说：「我要死了，但　神必与你们同在，领你们回到你们列祖之地。
verses.en: Then Israel said to Joseph, “I am about to die, but God will be with you[NOTE:1] and will bring you back to the land of your fathers.
notes: The pronouns translated “you,” “you,” and “your” in this verse are plural in the Hebrew text.
verses.commentary:
48:21 "Behold I am about to die, but God will be with you, and bring you back to the land of your
fathers" The "I" is emphatic. Jacob is the Patriarch. This is another allusion to the fact that the whole
family will be delivered from Egypt and that they will return to the Promised Land (cf. Gen. 15:12-16).

verses.zh: 并且我从前用弓用刀从亚摩利人手下夺的那块地，我都赐给你，使你比众弟兄多得一分。」
verses.en: As one who is above your[NOTE:1] brothers, I give to you the mountain slope,[NOTE:2] which I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow.”
notes: The pronouns translated “your” and “you” in this verse are singular in the Hebrew text.

The Hebrew word שְׁכֶם (shekhem) could be translated either as “mountain slope” or “shoulder, portion,” or even taken as the proper name “Shechem.” Jacob was giving Joseph either (1) one portion above his brothers, or (2) the mountain ridge he took from the Amorites, or (3) Shechem. The ambiguity actually allows for all three to be the referent. He could be referring to the land in Shechem he bought in Gen 33:18-19, but he mentions here that it was acquired by warfare, suggesting that the events of 34:25-29 are in view (even though at the time he denounced it, 34:30). Joseph was later buried in Shechem (Josh 24:32).
verses.commentary:
48:22 "I give you one portion more than your brothers" This term "portion" (BDB 1014 I) is literally
"shoulder" in Hebrew. It is the name of the city of Shechem. Some think it refers to this geographical
location because of the remainder of Gen. 48:22, which refers to the slaughter of the Shechemites, but this
seems unusual because in the book of Genesis this is such a negative act. Others say that the word "shoulder"
means that they were a stature higher, i.e. inherited more-the double inheritance of the firstborn. Some say
that it refers to Shechem being the territory which Ephraim will inherit and others say it refers to Shechem
being the site where Joseph will be buried (cf. Jos. 24:32). Manasseh will inherit on both sides of the
Jordan (the only tribe to do so). Ephraim will be the largest of the tribes in number and land allocation
(Judah second). Ephraim will dominate the northern part of Canaan, as Judah does the south. The leader, Joshua,
is from Ephraim, as is Samuel!

▣ "which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow" This seems to be a
historical event, but we do not have a record of it. The Rabbinical Midrash speculates that after the
slaughter of the Shechemites that the other Canaanite kings came against Jacob and that he defeated them
in battle. There is no record of this.

The term Amorite is a collective term to describe all of the Canaanite tribes
(cf. Gen. 15:16; Josh. 7:7; Jdgs. 6:10).
